written.myAnswer: Atomic number gives the correct order of elements and determines their electronic configuration, which explains their periodic properties. It also avoids the ordering anomalies that arise when elements are arranged by atomic mass.
“Periodic” means that the properties of elements recur at regular intervals when the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Periods become longer down the table because more subshells are available for filling in the higher principal energy levels, so they can accommodate more electrons and elements.
Elements in the same group have similar outermost-shell electron configurations, so they have the same number of valence electrons.
No. Sodium is more reactive than calcium because it loses its single outermost electron more readily.
Sodium has the largest atomic radius and chlorine the smallest in the third period.
The elements in Groups 16 and 17 are close to completing their outer shells: they need two and one electrons, respectively. They therefore attract electrons strongly and have high electronegativity.
Removing the first electron makes magnesium a positive ion, Mg⁺. Its remaining electrons are held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove the second electron.
Generally, no. Ionic bonds form by electron transfer, usually from a metal to a non-metal; two metals or two non-metals do not typically form an ionic bond with each other.
Francium has the least ionization energy, and fluorine has the highest electronegativity.
Use the element’s atomic number and electronic configuration to place it in the appropriate period and group of the periodic table.
Hydrogen is the first element. It can lose one electron or gain one electron.
Aluminium is expected to lose electrons more easily because its larger atomic radius means its outer electrons are farther from the nucleus.
For two identical bonded atoms, measure the distance between their nuclei; the atomic radius is half that distance.
Oxygen has six valence electrons and needs two more to complete its octet. Accepting three would give it more than an octet, so it does not form O³⁻ in the way nitrogen forms N³⁻.

Electronic configuration can be used to locate an element: its shells indicate the period and its valence electrons help indicate the group. Atomic mass is not a reliable substitute for atomic number.
There are four blocks: s, p, d and f. They help classify elements by the subshell being filled and relate to their properties.

Atomic radius generally decreases from left to right across a period because nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same shell, increasing the attraction between the nucleus and the electrons.
Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period because atomic radius decreases and the nucleus holds the outer electrons more strongly.
Electronegativity and ionization energy help predict bond type: they indicate how strongly an atom attracts electrons and how readily it loses them.
Carbon, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine.

The second and third periods each have two s-block and six p-block elements, giving eight elements. The first period has only the 1s subshell and two elements; the longer periods contain additional subshells, including d and, in the longest periods, f subshells.
The periodic table arranges elements systematically, reveals recurring patterns in their properties, and allows properties to be compared and predicted from an element’s position.

Lithium and beryllium differ from the other members of their groups partly because their atoms and ions are unusually small and have high charge density; they also have relatively high ionization energies.

Mendeleev arranged elements mainly by increasing atomic mass and chemical properties, whereas the modern periodic table arranges them by increasing atomic number. The modern arrangement explains periodicity through electronic configuration.
